flagged.doubt: Using the usual textbook weak-field treatment of H₂O gives a high-spin Co(III) complex. The hexaaquacobalt(III) ion is not a common stable textbook salt, so this species is less likely to be asked directly.

Using the usual textbook weak-field treatment of H₂O gives high-spin d⁶ Co(III), with unpaired electrons. The hexaaquacobalt(III) ion is not a common stable textbook salt, so this species is less likely to be asked directly.
Textbooks usually describe it as tetrahedral; the actual structure is often described as distorted tetrahedral.
This is the usual JEE/NCERT molecular VSEPR answer. Solid PCl₅ is described as [PCl₄]⁺[PCl₆]⁻, so it does not have a single molecular geometry.
Usual textbook assignment for molecular PCl₅; solid PCl₅ is ionic, as noted for its geometry.
Usual answer for symmetric molecular PCl₅. Solid PCl₅ is ionic, so molecular polarity is not applicable to the solid.
VSEPR gives AX2E2; I3+ is less commonly treated as a stable isolated species in standard JEE/NCERT material.
VSEPR gives four electron domains (AX2E2); I3+ is less commonly treated as a stable isolated species in standard JEE/NCERT material.
Usual JEE/NCERT electron-count treatment gives Cu(II), d⁹, and paramagnetism. Bulk CuO is antiferromagnetic below its Néel temperature, so its behavior depends on temperature.

The usual ionic textbook assignment is Cu(II), d⁹, hence paramagnetic. CuS (covellite) has more complex solid-state bonding and is not well described by this simple localized-ion model; JEE would generally use the ionic assignment or avoid this complication.

The textbook ionic assignment is high-spin Fe(II), hence paramagnetic. Bulk FeO has temperature-dependent magnetic ordering, which is not what the usual JEE unpaired-electron classification addresses.

The textbook ionic assignment is Fe(III), d⁵, hence paramagnetic. Bulk hematite has antiferromagnetic ordering (with weak ferromagnetism in some conditions); the JEE-style answer refers to the ionic/unpaired-electron classification.

In the usual textbook ionic treatment, NiS contains Ni²⁺ (d⁸), so it is paramagnetic. The solid has phase- and temperature-dependent magnetic ordering, which is not usually considered in JEE-style questions.

In crystalline Al(OH)₃, Al is octahedrally coordinated by O atoms. A simplified isolated-formula VSEPR treatment may give trigonal planar, but JEE would not normally ask the molecular geometry of this solid.
The usual coordination-sphere answer treats [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ as square planar. In the solid, additional axial contacts can distort or extend the coordination environment.
PH₄Br is treated as ionic phosphonium bromide; the geometry refers to the PH₄⁺ ion, not a P–Br bond.
SbOCl is a layered solid, not a discrete VSEPR molecule; its local coordination is not a standard JEE/NCERT geometry question, so this assignment is not a canonical answer-key value.
Bulk Al(OH)₃ has octahedrally coordinated Al, but hybridisation is not uniquely defined for this extended solid; a simple isolated-formula Lewis model may instead give sp2.
JEE-style steric-number treatment gives sp3; some accounts describe AsH3 bonding as nearly unhybridised p-orbital bonding.
Usually assigned from the dominant N≡N⁺–O⁻ Lewis structure; resonance makes a localized hybridisation label for O model-dependent.
PH₄Br is treated as ionic [PH₄]⁺Br⁻; P in [PH₄]⁺ is tetrahedral.

A simple formula-unit Lewis/VSEPR treatment gives sp2, but SbOCl is a solid with an extended structure, not a discrete molecule with a uniquely assignable central-atom hybridisation; JEE may not ask it this way.
The conventional textbook/JEE assignment for octahedral Te(OH)₆ is sp3d2.
[Zn(OH)₄]²⁻ is conventionally treated as a tetrahedral complex.
